Chapter 8. Cultivating Virtue: Living the Renaissance Values
Now that we've come this far on our journey, let’s turn our attention to something truly at the heart of Renaissance thinking—cultivating virtue.
What does that really mean? Well, virtues aren’t just lofty ideas—they’re practical, down-to-earth qualities that shape who we are and guide how we act.
Back in the Renaissance, thinkers identified all sorts of virtues—like courage, wisdom, humility, and generosity. Each one was brought to life through powerful archetypes, kind of like the characters you’ll find in the Mantegna Tarot.
So, how do you actually cultivate virtue? It’s all about intention and practice. Every day, it’s those small choices that add up—aligning what you do with what really matters to you. Over time, these choices become habits, and those habits shape your character. The Tarot can be a fantastic guide here, turning the pursuit of virtue into something you can see, feel, and work with every day.
Let’s talk about a few strategies for living out those Renaissance values in your own life:
First, there’s Virtue Mapping. This means figuring out which virtues matter most right now. Maybe you’re facing a challenge, or you’ve got a goal in mind. Pick an archetype from the Tarot that fits, and use it as your focus—just for today, or maybe for the whole week.
Next, think about Micro-Practices. Virtue doesn’t have to mean big, dramatic gestures. Break it down into small, doable steps. Want to practice patience? Try pausing before you answer someone. Looking to be more generous? Offer a kind word, or do a small act of service for someone. These little moments make a big difference over time.
Another approach is Reflective Tracking. Keep a journal. Jot down times when you lived out a virtue—or maybe when you missed the mark. This kind of reflection helps you notice patterns, reinforce what’s working, and gently spot areas where you can grow.
And don’t forget Community Engagement. The Renaissance wasn’t about going it alone. Virtue grows best in community—through conversations, shared rituals, or working together on projects that matter. Bring others into your journey; you’ll be surprised by how much deeper and more rewarding it becomes.
Want a real-world example? Imagine someone who wants to build courage. They might choose the Hero archetype and set small challenges: speaking up in a meeting, trying something new, or having that tough conversation they’ve been putting off. Bit by bit, those micro-practices build up genuine confidence and resilience.
Here’s the thing—cultivating virtue is a lifelong adventure. There will be progress, but also setbacks. The Renaissance spirit encourages us to be patient, forgiving with ourselves, and to keep a sense of humor along the way.
When you make virtue a daily practice, your life not only becomes more successful, but also more meaningful and fulfilling. And isn’t that what we’re all really after?
